segments.text: In {1923,|nineteen twenty three,} a radio officer at a London airport had to invent a way to scream for help. His answer was one word. Mayday.
His name was Frederick Mockford, at Croydon Airport. Pilots were moving from Morse code to talking over voice radio.
The old distress signal was SOS. But spoken over a crackly radio, the S could easily sound like an F.
Most of his flights went between London and Paris. So he borrowed from French. {M'aider.|Meh-day.} Help me.
Spelled the English way, it became Mayday. Nothing to do with the month of May.
Pilots say it three times. Mayday, Mayday, Mayday. So nobody mistakes it for someone just talking about one.
By {1927,|nineteen twenty seven,} it was the official distress call around the world.
It even has a little brother. Pan-pan, from the French panne, a breakdown. Serious, but not deadly yet.
So every Mayday you hear in the movies is really someone shouting help me, in French.
